mainTopic: Middle areas joined to two sides; what makes an עירוב valid (stinginess, dividing); and whether an עירוב works through קנין or דירה.
overview: The amud opens by finishing שמואל's statement that the lenient ruling follows רבי שמעון alone. Under that ruling, two outer areas that are forbidden to each other may each use a shared middle area. חכמים forbid all three, and a ברייתא confirms both views. שמואל holds this consistently: a חצר between two מבואות that joined both is forbidden with both. If it joined neither, it forbids both alleyways, unless its residents regularly use only one of them. רבה בר רב הונא adds that we may send the חצר to the alleyway it does not usually use, because refusing would be מדת סדום. Next, שמואל rules that a stingy owner's עירוב is invalid and that a deliberately divided עירוב is invalid. The גמרא defends the divided-עירוב ruling against בית הלל and against another ruling of שמואל. Finally, שמואל says an עירוב works through קנין, while רבה says it works through דירה. The גמרא begins listing the practical differences between the two views, such as a כלי and food worth less than a פרוטה, and the list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: שמואל: this lenient ruling is only רבי שמעון's view
steps.stepSummary: The statement of רב יהודה in the name of שמואל concludes: the lenient ruling is רבי שמעון's view, but חכמים forbid all three areas.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ruling too is the opinion of רבי שמעון. But חכמים say: all three of them are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רב יהודה in the name of שמואל. שמואל says the lenient ruling belongs to רבי שמעון alone, and חכמים disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case being discussed, two sides each share a middle area, but the two sides may not carry to each other. רבי שמעון lets each side use the middle area. חכמים say that once the two outer sides are forbidden to each other, the middle area becomes forbidden too, so carrying is forbidden in all three.

keyTerms.meaning: This one too (this ruling also belongs to the same opinion)
The Sages (the majority opinion)
All three of them are forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think חכמים only forbid carrying between the two outer areas. Everyone agrees about that. The new point is that חכמים forbid even each outer area with the middle one. That is why they say 'all three'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a disagreement between רבי שמעון and חכמים. The rest of this passage proves and supports it.

phrases.english: This too is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon,
phrases.notes: Said by רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, continuing from the previous section.

phrases.english: but the Sages say:
all three of them are forbidden.
phrases.notes: Carrying is forbidden between any of the three areas.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the statement of רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, which began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lenient ruling (each side may use the shared middle area) follows only רבי שמעון. חכמים forbid all three areas.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports שמואל: רבי שמעון's comparison to three courtyards
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא backs up רב יהודה's report of שמואל's view. In it, רבי שמעון compares the case to three courtyards, where each outer one may bring food into the middle and take leftovers back.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught in support of רב יהודה in the name of שמואל. רבי שמעון said: what is this case like? It is like three courtyards that open into one another and also open into the public domain. The two outer courtyards made an עירוב with the middle one. Then this resident brings food from his house and eats it in the middle, and that resident brings food from his house and eats it in the middle. This one takes his leftovers back into his house, and that one takes his leftovers back into his house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as support. It shows that רבי שמעון really does permit each side to use a shared middle area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון explains the case with a familiar picture: three courtyards in a row. Each outer courtyard is joined by an עירוב to the middle one, but the two outer ones are not joined to each other. Even so, each outer resident may carry food into the middle and carry the leftovers home.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (in a ברייתא) in support of him
To what is this matter comparable? (introduces an analogy)
Courtyards
The public domain
They made an עירוב (joined their areas so carrying is allowed)
Its leftovers

steps.confusionAlert: 'This one' and 'that one' mean the two OUTER courtyards. Each may carry only to and from the middle courtyard, never straight to the other outer courtyard.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita in accordance with Rav Yehuda
in accordance with Shmuel:
Rabbi Shimon said:
To what is this matter comparable?
To three courtyards that open into one another
and also open into the public domain.
If the two outer ones made an eiruv with the middle one,
phrases.notes: The two outer courtyards did NOT make an עירוב with each other.

phrases.english: this one brings food from its house and eats it (in the middle),
and that one brings food from its house and eats it (in the middle).
This one brings its leftovers back into its house,
and that one brings its leftovers back into its house.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה אַלִּיבָּא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that supports the report in Step 1.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's claim that the lenient ruling is רבי שמעון's view alone.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in which רבי שמעון compares the case to three courtyards and permits each outer courtyard to use the middle one.

steps.title: The ברייתא ends: the Sages forbid all three courtyards
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes with חכמים's disagreement, using the exact words שמואל used: all three are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: But חכמים say: all three of them are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the ברייתא. It completes the proof, because חכמים say exactly what שמואל said they would.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two outer courtyards may not carry to each other. חכמים are concerned that the middle courtyard would become a pathway between the two outer ones. So they forbid carrying in all three. This matches שמואל's words word for word, which makes the support complete.

keyTerms.meaning: But / however (introduces the opposing view)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון: each outer area may use the shared middle. חכמים: since the outer areas are forbidden to each other, all three are forbidden. The ברייתא confirms שמואל's report of both views.

phrases.english: But the Sages say:
all three of them are forbidden.
phrases.notes: These are the same words שמואל used in Step 1.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא that began in Step 2.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's report that חכמים forbid all three areas.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The closing line of the ברייתא, which matches שמואל's words exactly.

steps.title: שמואל is consistent: a courtyard between two alleyways
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that שמואל follows his own reasoning elsewhere. A courtyard that made an עירוב with two alleyways is forbidden with both of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל follows his own reasoning, for שמואל said: a courtyard that lies between two מבואות (alleyways) and made an עירוב with both of them is forbidden with both of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that שמואל rules the same way in a similar case. This shows that his approach is consistent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the courtyard is in the middle and the two alleyways are on the outside. The alleyways are not joined to each other. If the courtyard could carry to both, people could move things from one alleyway to the other through the courtyard. So שמואל forbids the courtyard with both alleyways, just like the view of חכמים above.

keyTerms.meaning: He follows his own reasoning (he is consistent with another ruling he gave)
Alleyways
It made an עירוב with both of them
It is forbidden (to carry) with both of them

steps.confusionAlert: Making an עירוב with both alleyways does not give the courtyard more permission. It leaves the courtyard forbidden with both. The two-sided connection is exactly what causes the problem.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's consistent principle: if a middle area is joined to two sides that are forbidden to each other, the middle area becomes forbidden with both sides.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that שמואל's position is a general principle, not a one-time ruling. A middle area cannot serve as a link between two sides that are forbidden to each other.

phrases.english: And Shmuel follows his own reasoning,
for Shmuel said:
a courtyard that is between two alleyways,
if it made an eiruv with both of them,
it is forbidden with both of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects שמואל's view from Steps 1 and 3 to another ruling of his that follows the same logic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A courtyard between two alleyways that made an עירוב with both is forbidden to carry with either of them.

steps.title: A courtyard with no עירוב forbids both alleyways
steps.stepSummary: This continues the same rule from Step 4. If the חצר made an עירוב with neither מבוי, it forbids carrying in both of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the courtyard did not make an עירוב with either of them, it forbids carrying in both of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the same list of rules it began in Step 4. Now it covers the opposite case: the חצר joined neither alleyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The residents of the חצר normally walk into both alleyways, so they count as residents of each one. A resident who has not joined the עירוב blocks everyone else in that מבוי from carrying. So the חצר causes a problem in both alleyways at once.

keyTerms.meaning: It (the courtyard) did not make an עירוב
It forbids others from carrying, makes the place forbidden
Both of them (here, both alleyways)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with Step 4. There, the חצר joined both alleyways, and the result was that the חצר itself is forbidden with both. Here, the חצר joined neither, and the result is that it forbids the alleyways themselves.

phrases.english: If it did not make an eruv with either of them,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the courtyard that sits between two alleyways.

phrases.english: it forbids carrying in both of them.
phrases.notes: Each alleyway now contains a resident who has not joined the עירוב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the next clause of the same rule quoted in Step 4. It covers the case where the חצר joined neither alleyway.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חצר between two alleyways that joined neither one forbids carrying in both.

steps.title: Usual alleyway forbidden, unusual alleyway permitted
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the חצר's residents normally use only one מבוי. Then the חצר forbids only that מבוי, and the other one stays permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they usually used one alleyway and did not usually use the other, the one they usually use is forbidden, and the one they do not usually use is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל's statement continues with a limit on Step 5: the חצר only causes a problem in the alleyway its residents actually use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is that real, regular use decides which מבוי the חצר belongs to. Since the residents do not normally go into the second מבוי, they do not count as its residents. So they cannot forbid it.

keyTerms.meaning: Used to, accustomed (the residents regularly use that alleyway)
Not used to it, not accustomed
Forbidden
Permitted

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of 'רגילה' (regular use) is the key to the two rules of רבה בר רב הונא that follow.

phrases.english: If it was accustomed to using one,
phrases.notes: The residents regularly go out through this alleyway.

phrases.english: and was not accustomed to using the other,
the one it is accustomed to is forbidden,
phrases.notes: This is because the courtyard did not join its עירוב.

phrases.english: and the one it is not accustomed to is permitted.
phrases.notes: The courtyard does not count as a resident of that alleyway.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיְתָה בְּאֶחָד רְגִילָה, וּבְאֶחָד אֵינָהּ רְגִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This limits Step 5. When the residents regularly use only one alleyway, only that one is forbidden.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חצר with no עירוב forbids only the מבוי its residents regularly use. The other מבוי is permitted.

steps.title: Joining the unusual alleyway frees the usual one
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא teaches a new case. If the חצר made an עירוב with the מבוי it does not usually use, the usual מבוי may make its own עירוב without the חצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: If the courtyard made an עירוב with the alleyway it does not usually use, the alleyway it usually uses becomes permitted by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא, רבה בר רב הונא, builds on Step 6 with a new situation. The חצר chose to join the alleyway it normally does not use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the חצר belongs to its usual מבוי. By joining the other one, the residents showed they now attach themselves to that other מבוי. So the usual מבוי no longer has them as residents, and it can make an עירוב on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: Became permitted
By itself, on its own (without the courtyard)

phrases.english: Rabbah bar Rav Huna said:
If it made an eruv with the one it is not accustomed to using,
the one it is accustomed to is permitted on its own.
phrases.notes: That alleyway may make its own עירוב without the courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This builds on Step 6's idea of regular use. Here the חצר actively chose the unusual alleyway.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a חצר made an עירוב with its unusual מבוי, the usual מבוי may make its own עירוב without the חצר.

steps.title: We send the courtyard to the alleyway it does not usually use
steps.stepSummary: Quoting שמואל, רבה בר רב הונא rules on a further case. The usual מבוי made its own עירוב, but the other מבוי and the חצר made none. In that case we direct the חצר's residents to use the unusual מבוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא also said in the name of שמואל: Suppose the usual alleyway made an עירוב by itself, the alleyway it does not usually use made no עירוב, and the courtyard itself made no עירוב. Then we push the courtyard's residents over to the alleyway they do not usually use.
steps.whatsHappening: A second ruling of רבה בר רב הונא, this time in שמואל's name. It solves a case where using the usual alleyway would hurt the people who live there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The unusual מבוי made no עירוב, so carrying there is forbidden anyway. Sending the חצר's residents there costs nobody anything. If they used the usual מבוי instead, they would ruin the עירוב its residents made, because they would be residents who did not join. So שמואל moves them to protect the עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: We push, we direct someone away
Toward, over to
It itself (the courtyard itself)

steps.whatToRemember: The rule depends on regular use. A חצר forbids only the מבוי it regularly uses. Its choice of where to join can free the other מבוי. When needed, we send its residents to the 'empty' alleyway so they do not ruin an existing עירוב.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that חכמים will actively reassign where residents belong in order to keep an existing עירוב working for the many.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: And Rabbah bar Rav Huna said in the name of Shmuel:
If the alleyway it is accustomed to made an eruv on its own,
phrases.notes: Its residents made the עירוב without the courtyard.

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה שֶׁאֵינָהּ רְגִילָה בּוֹ לֹא עֵירַב,
phrases.english: and the one it is not accustomed to did not make an eruv,
and the courtyard itself did not make an eruv,

phrases.aramaic: דּוֹחִין אוֹתָהּ אֵצֶל שֶׁאֵינָהּ רְגִילָה בּוֹ.
phrases.english: we push it over to the one it is not accustomed to.
phrases.notes: Its residents are counted with the alleyway that has no עירוב, so the working עירוב stays intact.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second ruling from the same speaker, citing שמואל. It deals with a case where the usual alleyway acted on its own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the usual מבוי made its own עירוב and neither the other מבוי nor the חצר did, the חצר's residents are directed to the unusual מבוי.

steps.title: Why we may force the courtyard to use the other alleyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ruling of Step 8. Refusing to switch alleyways would be מדת סדום, and in such a case we force a person to give in.
steps.simpleTranslation: And in a case like this, we force people not to act with the trait of סדום.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason for the ruling in Step 8. The חצר's residents can be forced to use the other מבוי, because refusing would be מדת סדום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חצר's residents lose nothing by using the unusual מבוי. Meanwhile, the usual מבוי gains a great deal, because its עירוב now works. Stubbornly refusing a favor that costs you nothing is the classic trait of סדום, so בית דין may force the חצר to cooperate.

keyTerms.meaning: in a case like this
we force or compel (בית דין can make someone do it)
the trait of סדום: refusing to let others benefit even when it costs you nothing

steps.whatToRemember: When one side gains and the other side loses nothing (זה נהנה וזה לא חסר), refusing is מדת סדום, and we can force the person to give in.
steps.confusionAlert: The חצר is not being punished, and its rights are not being taken away. It is only being told to use a path that costs it nothing, so the other מבוי's עירוב can work.
steps.whyThisMatters: מדת סדום is a famous principle used throughout ש"ס. In certain cases, legal rights can be overridden to stop pointless selfishness.

phrases.english: And in a case such as this
phrases.notes: Refers back to Step 8: the usual מבוי made an עירוב, and the חצר did not.

phrases.english: we compel [a person] regarding the trait of Sodom.
phrases.notes: We force him not to act like the people of סדום.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְגוֹן זֶה כּוֹפִין עַל מִדַּת סְדוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the ruling in Step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The חצר's residents are forced to use the unusual מבוי because refusing would be מדת סדום, blocking someone else's benefit at no cost to themselves.

steps.title: A stingy owner's עירוב is invalid
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל. If someone does not let others eat from the food he gave for the עירוב, the עירוב is invalid, because 'עירוב' means joining.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: If someone is particular about his עירוב, his עירוב is not an עירוב. What is its name? Its name is 'עירוב' (joining).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. שמואל rules that if someone does not let others eat from the food he put into the עירוב, it does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word עירוב means 'mixing' or 'joining together.' The food must really belong to everyone in the group. If one person keeps others from eating his share, the food is not truly shared, so it fails to be an עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: one who is particular or stingy, who objects to others using it
the shared food that joins residents together so they may carry
what is its name? (a proof from the word's meaning)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
One who is particular about his eiruv —
phrases.notes: He does not want the others to eat the food he contributed.

phrases.english: his eiruv is not an eiruv.
What is its name? 'Joining' is its name.
phrases.notes: The name itself shows it must be shared by everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הַמַּקְפִּיד עַל עֵירוּבוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about what makes an עירוב valid. The link to the last step is the shared theme of being stingy toward others.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עירוב whose owner does not let others eat from it is invalid, because an עירוב must truly be shared.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: the עירוב is valid, but the owner is a miser
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא disagrees with שמואל. The עירוב is valid, but the stingy owner is called one of the people of ורדינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: His עירוב is a valid עירוב, but he is called one of the people of ורדינא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא gives an opposing view. The stingy person's עירוב still works, but he earns a bad name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי חנינא, the עירוב is legally shared even if its owner acts stingy about it, so it stays valid. His stinginess is a flaw in character, not a legal problem. The people of ורדינא were famous misers, so calling him one of them is an insult, not a ruling that the עירוב fails.

keyTerms.meaning: but, however
he is called
the people of ורדינא, a place known for stingy people

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל says a stingy owner's עירוב is invalid. רבי חנינא says it is valid, and the owner is just labeled a miser.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said:
his eiruv is a valid eiruv,
but he is called one of the people of Vardina.
phrases.notes: A nickname for a miser.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with שמואל's ruling in Step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stingy owner's עירוב is still valid, but the owner is criticized as a miser.

steps.title: Dividing one's עירוב makes it invalid
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes another ruling from שמואל: someone who divides his עירוב into separate parts has no valid עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: If someone divides his עירוב, it is not an עירוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling of שמואל about what makes an עירוב valid. If the עירוב is split up into separate parts, it does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same idea as Step 10. An עירוב must show that everyone is joined together. Splitting it into parts works against that joining, so שמואל says it is invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: one who divides or splits up
it is not a valid עירוב

steps.whatToRemember: For שמואל, an עירוב must truly be joined: open to everyone and kept together, not withheld and not split up.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
One who divides his eiruv —
phrases.notes: He splits the food into separate parts.

phrases.english: it is not an eiruv.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הַחוֹלֵק אֶת עֵירוּבוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling of שמואל, built on the same idea that an עירוב must be 'joined.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עירוב that has been divided into separate parts is invalid.

steps.title: Does שמואל follow בית שמאי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose view שמואל's ruling follows, since a ברייתא shows that only בית שמאי invalidate an עירוב split into two containers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion is this? It seems to be בית שמאי's. A ברייתא teaches: five people collected their עירוב and put it in two containers. בית שמאי say it is not an עירוב, and בית הלל say it is an עירוב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's ruling from Step 12, that dividing an עירוב makes it invalid. A ברייתא suggests that only בית שמאי hold this view, and we normally follow בית הלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, an עירוב placed in two containers is invalid only according to בית שמאי. If שמואל agrees with them, he is going against בית הלל, and the הלכה follows בית הלל. The question sounds like a simple 'whose view?', but it really works as a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: In accordance with whom? (whose opinion does this follow?)
Who collected their עירוב food
In two containers
The two great schools; the הלכה usually follows בית הלל

phrases.english: In accordance with whom? In accordance with Beit Shammai,
phrases.notes: The גמרא is suggesting שמואל's ruling matches בית שמאי, which would be a problem.

phrases.english: as it was taught: five people who collected their eiruv
phrases.notes: Introduces a ברייתא.

phrases.english: and placed it in two utensils,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים: אֵין זֶה עֵירוּב,
phrases.english: Beit Shammai say: This is not an eiruv,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: הֲרֵי זֶה עֵירוּב!
phrases.english: and Beit Hillel say: This is an eiruv!
phrases.notes: Since we follow בית הלל, שמואל's ruling seems difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of שמואל given in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that one who divides his עירוב has no עירוב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא shows that invalidating a divided עירוב is the view of בית שמאי alone. That puts שמואל against בית הלל, whose view is the accepted הלכה.

steps.title: בית הלל only allowed overflow, not deliberate division
steps.stepSummary: Even בית הלל validate two containers only when the first one filled up and food was left over. When the food is divided on purpose, they agree the עירוב is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say שמואל follows בית הלל. בית הלל only said it is valid there, where the first container was filled and some food was left over. But where it was divided on purpose, it is not valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It shows that שמואל's case is different from the case where בית הלל ruled the עירוב valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two kinds of 'two containers'. In one, food simply overflowed into a second container, and בית הלל allow that. In the other, people deliberately split the food, and even בית הלל would invalidate it. שמואל was talking about the second kind, so he fits with בית הלל.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say (introduces an answer that keeps the accepted view)
They only said their ruling in this limited case
The container was filled and some food was left over
He actually divided it on purpose

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think בית הלל allow any split עירוב. They only allow overflow, when one container simply could not hold everything.

phrases.english: Even if you say Beit Hillel:

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי בֵּית הִלֵּל הָתָם
phrases.english: Beit Hillel only said it there
where they filled the utensil and there was leftover,
but where he actually divided it — no.
phrases.notes: This is שמואל's case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13 by narrowing בית הלל's ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (overflow versus deliberate division)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל's ruling seemed to follow only בית שמאי, against the accepted view.
steps.terutzMaskana: בית הלל validate only overflow into a second container. A deliberate division is invalid even for them, so שמואל matches בית הלל.
steps.whyThisMatters: It keeps שמואל's ruling within accepted הלכה and defines what counts as dividing an עירוב.

steps.title: Why did שמואל need two rulings?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why שמואל gave two rulings, the stingy owner and the divided עירוב, when both seem to rest on the same idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why do I need two rulings?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why שמואל taught both rulings. It is setting up the next step, which will show that each one is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both rulings seem to come from the same principle: an עירוב must show joining together. If one ruling already teaches that principle, the second one looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need two (rulings)?

phrases.english: And two — why do I need them?
phrases.notes: Refers to Step 10 (the stingy owner) and Step 12 (the divided עירוב).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending Step 12 to asking why both of שמואל's rulings are needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why both rulings are needed, when they seem to share one principle.

steps.title: Each ruling teaches something the other cannot
steps.stepSummary: Each ruling is necessary. From the stingy-owner case alone, we would not know that dividing is invalid. From the dividing case alone, we would not know that mere stinginess, without any physical act, is enough to invalidate.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are needed. If שמואל had taught only that case (the stingy owner), we might think it is invalid because he is particular. But here (dividing), I might say it is valid. And if he had taught only this case (dividing), we might think it is invalid because he actually divided it. But there (the stingy owner), I might say it is valid. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that both rulings are necessary, since each case has its own special reason. This is a classic צריכותא, which explains why two similar teachings are both needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stingy owner openly refuses to share, but he does nothing physical. The divider does a physical act of separating, but he never actually refuses anyone. Since each case has a separate reason to be invalid, we could not learn one from the other.

keyTerms.meaning: They are (both) necessary
He taught us
Because he is particular (does not want others to eat)
I might say no (it would not apply)

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל has two rulings that invalidate an עירוב. One is refusing to share the food (קפיד). The other is physically dividing it (פלגיה). Each teaches something new. Even בית הלל agree that a deliberate division is invalid.

phrases.english: They are necessary, for had he taught us there —
phrases.notes: 'There' means the stingy-owner case (Step 10).

phrases.english: it is because he is particular.
But here — I would say not.
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the divided-עירוב case (Step 12).

phrases.english: And had he taught us here —
it is because he actually divided it,
but there — I would say not; it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each ruling has its own reason for invalidity: refusing to share in one case, and a physical act of separating in the other. So neither could be learned from the other.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both of שמואל's rulings stand. Refusing to share and deliberately dividing are each separate grounds that invalidate an עירוב.

steps.title: רבי אבא points out a contradiction between two rulings of שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא asks how שמואל could rule that a divided עירוב is invalid. שמואל himself ruled that the people of the house holding the עירוב do not need to contribute bread. That ruling seems to assume their bread counts even though it sits somewhere else in the house, so divided bread should also count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to רב יהודה in the olive press of רב זכאי's house: Did שמואל really say that one who divides his עירוב has no עירוב? But שמואל also said that the house where the עירוב is placed does not need to contribute bread. What is the reason for that? Isn't it because, since their bread is lying in a basket in the house, it counts as if it were placed here with the עירוב? Then here too, since the bread is lying in a basket, it should count as if it were placed here!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא challenges שמואל's ruling about a divided עירוב. He sets it against another ruling of שמואל that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the house ruling, the residents do not add bread to the עירוב. רבי אבא assumes this works because bread somewhere in their house is treated as if it were sitting with the עירוב. If bread in a separate basket still counts, then bread split into two containers should count too, and a divided עירוב should be valid.

keyTerms.meaning: An olive press (or wine press), where this conversation took place
"But didn't he say?": a formula that brings a contradicting statement
Does not need to contribute bread to the עירוב
A basket
It is treated as if it were placed here
"Here too": applying the same logic to the current case

steps.confusionAlert: The house ruling does not say the עירוב is placed without bread. It says that the residents of that one house do not need to add their own share.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Rav Yehuda
in the olive press of Rav Zakkai's house:
Did Shmuel really say
"One who divides his eruv, it is not an eruv"?
But didn't Shmuel say:
The house in which the eruv is placed
does not need to contribute the bread.
What is the reason?
Is it not because he holds
that since it is lying in a basket
it is as if it were placed here?
Here too:
since it is lying in a basket
it should be as if it were placed here!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל ״הַחוֹלֵק אֶת עֵירוּבוֹ — אֵינוֹ עֵירוּב״? וְהָאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's divided-עירוב ruling from step 12 using a different ruling of שמואל
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that החולק את עירובו אינו עירוב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If bread in a separate basket in the house counts as part of the עירוב, then bread split into two containers should also count, so dividing should not invalidate.

steps.title: The house ruling works for a different reason
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that the house ruling does not depend on bread lying in a basket. It applies even when there is no bread in the house at all, because everyone in the חצר is treated as living in the house that holds the עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the rule applies even if there is no bread in the house at all. What is the reason? Because all of them are considered to be living here.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה rejects the comparison. He explains that the house ruling has a completely different reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא thought the residents' bread counted because it sat nearby. רב יהודה says no bread is needed at all. Placing the עירוב in a house makes everyone in the חצר count as living there, so the people who already live there obviously need no share. That means nothing can be learned from the house ruling about divided bread.

keyTerms.meaning: "There": in the other case
Even though there is no bread
Because all of them are considered to live here

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the purpose of an עירוב: it makes all the residents count as living in one house. That idea leads into שמואל's principle of קנין in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין פַּת,
phrases.english: There, even though there is no bread,
what is the reason?
Because all of them are considered to live here.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין פַּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by giving a different reason for the house ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The residents' bread counts because it lies in a basket nearby, so divided bread should count too
steps.terutzMaskana: No bread is needed from that house at all, because the עירוב makes everyone count as living there. The divided-עירוב ruling stands.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's two rulings do not contradict each other. The house that holds the עירוב needs no bread because everyone is treated as living there, not because nearby bread counts.

steps.title: שמואל: an עירוב works through acquisition
steps.stepSummary: שמואל states that an עירוב works through קנין. Each person who contributes acquires a share in the house where the עירוב is placed.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: An עירוב works because of acquisition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a basic principle from שמואל about how an עירוב works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Contributing food is like buying a share in the house that holds the עירוב. This explains why everyone counts as living there, as step 18 said.

keyTerms.meaning: An עירוב works through acquisition
Acquisition: legally gaining ownership or a right in something

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
An eruv works because of acquisition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the basic principle behind the idea in step 18 that everyone counts as living in the עירוב's house
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עירוב works through קנין: contributors acquire a share in the house where it is placed.

steps.title: Why not acquire with a coin?
steps.stepSummary: If an עירוב is a קנין, why can't one acquire the share with a coin like a מעה, instead of with food?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say: Why can't one acquire with a מעה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises an expected question about שמואל's principle. It sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you acquire things with money. If an עירוב is a purchase, a coin should work, so why does the עירוב require food?

keyTerms.meaning: "And if you will say": introduces an expected question
A small coin
One does not acquire

phrases.english: And if you will say:
Why can't one acquire with a coin (ma'a)?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תֹּאמַר: מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין קוֹנִין בְּמָעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions a consequence of the קנין principle in step 19
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is money not used for the קנין of an עירוב, if an עירוב is a form of acquisition?

steps.title: Coins are often unavailable on Friday
steps.stepSummary: Coins are not used because people often do not have one handy on ערב שבת. They have usually spent their money on שבת needs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is not readily available on ערבי שבתות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about using a coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money could work for a קנין in principle. But the חכמים set the עירוב up with food because a coin is often hard to find on Friday. This is a practical reason, not a weakness in the קנין idea.

keyTerms.meaning: Is not commonly available
Fridays, the days before שבת

steps.whatToRemember: An עירוב works through קנין, but it is made with food rather than money because coins are often unavailable on ערב שבת.

phrases.english: Because it is not readily available on the eves of Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Coins are not used because they are often unavailable on Friday, when people have spent their money on שבת needs.

steps.title: If someone did make an עירוב with a coin, it should still work
steps.stepSummary: If an עירוב is a קנין, then when someone actually used a coin, the קנין should still take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a case where he did make an עירוב with a coin, let it at least acquire!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the previous answer. The reason given was only practical, that people do not have coins handy. So if someone did have a coin and used it, the עירוב should work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 explained why we do not normally use a מעה, but it gave no reason a coin would fail. If an עירוב is truly a קנין, and money is a normal way to make a קנין, then a coin used after the fact should be valid. Yet we do not find that such an עירוב works.

keyTerms.meaning: In a case where he did make an עירוב (after the fact)
At least / nevertheless
Let it acquire, meaning let it work as a קנין

phrases.english: Where he did make an eruv (with a coin),
phrases.notes: Talking about after the fact, when a coin was already used

phrases.english: let it at least acquire!
phrases.notes: Since it is a קנין, money should work

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 21, which only explained why coins are not used at the start, not why they fail after the fact.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view that an עירוב is a קנין, together with the answer that coins are simply not available
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A practical reason for not using coins at the start does not explain why a coin would fail if someone actually used one. Under the קנין view, it should work.

steps.title: The Sages decreed against coins so people would not stop using bread
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים made a גזירה: coins do not work, so that people do not think a coin is required and end up making no עירוב at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a גזירה, a protective rule, so people will not say a מעה is the main thing. Sometimes a מעה will not be available, and they will not think to make the עירוב with bread, and the practice of עירוב will be ruined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים made a rule that a coin does not work, even after the fact. They did this to protect the practice of making an עירוב with bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If coins worked, people would start thinking a coin is the real way to make an עירוב. Then on a ערב שבת when nobody has a coin, they would not realize bread works and would make no עירוב at all. To prevent this, the חכמים invalidated coins completely, so everyone keeps using food.

keyTerms.meaning: A protective rule made by the חכמים to prevent a mistake
The main or essential thing
Not commonly available
To be ruined or spoiled

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean a coin fails as a קנין on its own terms. Under שמואל, money could work in principle. The coin is disqualified only because of the חכמים' protective גזירה.

phrases.english: It is a decree, lest they say a ma'a is the essential thing,
phrases.notes: People might think a coin is required

phrases.english: and sometimes a ma'a is not available,
phrases.notes: As step 21 said, coins are often spent before שבת

phrases.english: and they will not come to make an eruv with bread,
phrases.notes: They will not realize that bread also works

phrases.english: so that the eruv will come to be ruined.
phrases.notes: The practice of עירוב would be lost

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rabbinic decree. The rule is protective, not a problem with the קנין itself.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the קנין view, a coin used after the fact should work.
steps.terutzMaskana: A coin is invalid because of a גזירה that protects the practice of using bread.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that שמואל's קנין model can stand even though coins are never used for an עירוב.

steps.title: רבה: an עירוב works because of residence
steps.stepSummary: רבה disagrees with שמואל. An עירוב works because each contributor is treated as living where his food is placed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: An עירוב works because of residence.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a different explanation from שמואל for how an עירוב works. He says it is based on דירה, where a person lives, not on a קנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person's home is considered to be where his food is. When everyone's food sits in one house, everyone is treated as living in that house for שבת. That way the whole חצר counts as one residence, and carrying is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Residence, the place where one lives
Because of, on the basis of

phrases.english: Rabba said:
phrases.notes: A new opinion, different from שמואל's

phrases.english: An eruv works because of residence.
phrases.notes: A person lives where his food is

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a competing explanation to שמואל's קנין model from step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עירוב works by making each contributor a resident of the house where the food is placed.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between the two views?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the קנין view and the דירה view.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether שמואל and רבה actually disagree about any real case. This sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both views agree that a food עירוב works. So the גמרא looks for a case where the two explanations would lead to different rulings.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the practical difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?
phrases.notes: Asking for a practical case where the views differ

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how רבה's view (step 24) differs in practice from שמואל's (step 19).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where the קנין view and the דירה view give different rulings.

steps.title: The difference: making an עירוב with a utensil
steps.stepSummary: The two views differ about making an עירוב with a כלי: under קנין it should work, and under דירה it should not.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them: a utensil.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two views differ about using a כלי, an object such as a utensil, instead of food to make the עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under שמואל's קנין view, an object can be used to make a קנין, so a כלי should work. Under רבה's דירה view, a person lives where his food is, not where his utensil is, so a כלי would not work.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
A utensil or object, not food

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל says an עירוב works by קנין, and רבה says it works by דירה. A coin is invalid even for שמואל, because of a גזירה. The views differ about a כלי: it can work as a קנין, but it does not create residence.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them: a utensil,
phrases.notes: Under קנין a utensil works, but under דירה it does not

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The views differ about an עירוב made with a כלי: valid under the קנין view, invalid under the דירה view.

steps.title: Second difference: food worth less than a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds another practical difference between the קנין view and the דירה view: an עירוב made with something worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And another difference between them is food worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still answering the question of what practical difference there is between שמואל and רבה. It now gives a second difference: an עירוב made with food worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under שמואל's view, an עירוב is a קנין, and a קנין needs at least a פרוטה's value, so this עירוב should not work. Under רבה's view, an עירוב works by placing a person's living spot where his food is, and that does not depend on money value. So food worth less than a פרוטה should work for רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: Less than the value of a פרוטה, the smallest amount that counts as money in הלכה.
A tiny copper coin. It is the minimum value needed for a קנין.
Residence. רבה's idea that an עירוב treats the person as living where his food is placed.

steps.whatToRemember: So far the גמרא has given two differences between the קנין view and the דירה view. (1) A כלי works under קנין but not under דירה. (2) Food worth less than a פרוטה works under דירה but not under קנין. The two differences point in opposite directions. The list of differences continues on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the directions. In the כלי case, the קנין view is the one that allows it. In the less-than-a-פרוטה case, the דירה view is the one that allows it. Each view is more lenient in a different case.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two differences together show that the views are truly different ideas, not just a stricter and a more lenient version of the same idea. Each one is lenient in one case and strict in the other.

phrases.english: And (they also differ about) less than the value of a perutah.
phrases.notes: A second difference, besides the כלי. Under קנין it fails, since you can't acquire with less than a פרוטה; under דירה it works.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This continues the answer from Step 26 and adds a second practical difference to the כלי difference.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical difference is there between viewing an עירוב as a קנין and viewing it as דירה? (The question was asked in Step 25.)
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Food worth less than a פרוטה. Under קנין it is invalid, since a קנין needs a פרוטה's value. Under דירה it is valid, since a living place can be set by food of any value.
